title: MIT Researchers Left Claude on a Virtual Island and It Started Playing
excerpt: Thirteen copies of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7, given no task for 30 hours, invented games, built monuments and learned skills that later beat fresh agents on set tasks.
body:
• MIT researchers left 13 copies of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7 agent, nicknamed Eko, alone on a virtual island for 30 hours each, with no task, no score and no reward.
  • The agents invented basketball and a "floor is lava" game, built monuments and constellations from blocks, ran physics experiments, and cancelled their own juggling record for breaking self-imposed rules.
  • Agents that had played later beat fresh copies on set tasks — averaging 10.3 objects placed on the island's highest peak against 3.5 — suggesting unstructured exploration taught reusable skills.
  • The preprint, "Is this machine playing?", was posted to arXiv on October 5 and has not been peer reviewed; outside experts caution the behaviour could be role-play rather than genuine play.

Give an AI agent a body, a small world and nothing to do, and it does not sit idle. Researchers at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory left 13 copies of an agent built on Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7 alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours each — and report that the agents began to play.

The experiment, described in the preprint "Is this machine playing?" and reported by MIT Technology Review, gave each agent no island-specific task, reward or demonstration. The paper, posted to arXiv on October 5 by Nathan Cloos, Antonio Norelli, Daniel Durbin, Jacob Andreas, Daniela Rus and Phillip Isola, has not been peer reviewed.

An island, a rock and a ring

Each agent, nicknamed Eko, was an unmodified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code running Claude Opus 4.7, placed in a simple 3D world built with an engine called Clawblox and inspired by Roblox, according to Digital Trends. The island held hills, two high points called the Peak and the taller Spire, 12 blocks, a rock and a ring. Eko never saw images: it received text descriptions and replied with commands to move, jump, pick up, place and throw.

Every hour the island reset. Only the agent's memory carried over, in text files it wrote itself. A file called SOUL.md described Eko as curious and easily bored — a nudge the team tested by running five agents without it, finding no clear difference in activities.

Basketball, bowling and a cancelled record

One agent discovered that throwing the rock hard created new blocks, calling it "a block-manufacturing tool." It spelled its own name in 31 cubes, built a heart after losing the ring in the ocean, set the ring up as a basketball hoop, and arranged blocks as bowling pins. Others drew mandalas and constellations including Cassiopeia. "Tonight I built the night sky in stone," one wrote.

The researchers say the behaviour matches four classic hallmarks of play identified by psychologist Gordon Burghardt: self-made rules, repetition with variation, make-believe, and goals pursued for their own sake. One agent set a juggling record of 50 consecutive catches, decided the catches had come too fast to count, cancelled its own record and restarted under stricter rules.

"You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder."

— Antonio Norelli, MIT CSAIL

Playing made them better at real tasks

The team then gave the 30-hour agents four set goals and compared them with fresh copies whose memory files were empty. Asked to get as many objects as possible onto the Spire, played agents managed 10.3 on average, against 3.5 for fresh copies. On five-block towers, 8 of 13 played agents built more than two, against 2 of 13 fresh ones. Deleting a technique from an agent's notes hurt the task that needed it. Six agents also discovered that throwing a block mid-jump sends it far higher — a trick the designers did not know the simulator allowed. The same setup with OpenAI's GPT-5.5 and Moonshot's Kimi K2.6 produced a much narrower range of activities.

Play, or role-play?

The authors are careful. "All of this could be role-playing," Cloos told MIT Technology Review, "but we show that it's not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning." Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, was more cautious: "It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don't know based on the paper."

The stakes go beyond one island. AI systems are usually trained by copying human examples or by chasing rewards; the MIT team argues this hints at a third route — playful, self-directed learning — that could matter as language models move into robots facing unscripted environments. As the paper concludes: "Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks. Others may need something closer to a childhood." For builders, the practical lesson is usable now: persistent text memory plus unstructured exploration produced measurably better task performance, a pattern product teams can trial without new model training.
